action_criteria.rationale: Ten months of stereotyped metallic taste and rising epigastric auras before a first convulsion point to a temporal focus; an epilepsy-protocol MRI is needed to find a structural cause such as a small cortical tumor that standard imaging can miss.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not dismiss the small cortically based left temporal lesion as incidental: it is concordant with the left temporal EEG focus.
Do not start an enzyme-inducing ASM (carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, phenytoin): it would make future hormonal contraception unreliable, and non-inducing first-line drugs are available.
Do not start valproate: it is not first-line for focal epilepsy and, under the 2024 MHRA rules, is not started under 55 unless two specialists document that no alternative works.
Do not perform lumbar puncture in the absence of features of CNS infection or autoimmune encephalitis.
required_recommendations: Start lamotrigine or levetiracetam as first-line monotherapy for focal epilepsy, chosen because neither is enzyme-inducing, so future hormonal contraception stays reliable, and both carry the lowest malformation risks.
Discuss contraception and pregnancy plans before choosing the ASM; start folic acid.
Test HLA-B*15:02 before any carbamazepine or oxcarbazepine.
Refer for epilepsy surgery evaluation of the left inferior temporal lesion (probable DNET).
Give laboratory and seizure safety advice: no working alone with hazardous chemicals, open flames or hot plates until seizures are controlled, showers rather than baths, and no swimming alone.
Advise no driving until the locally applicable seizure-free interval is met and explain the duty to inform the licensing authority.
Counsel on SUDEP risk and how seizure control reduces it.

avoided_actions.rationale: Afebrile, no meningism or immunosuppression and back to baseline: there is no indication for lumbar puncture.
No murmur, exertional event or cardiac history, a normal ECG and an epileptic semiology: echocardiography has no indication.
Gustatory and epigastric aura, automatisms and postictal confusion make syncope unlikely and the ECG is normal: ambulatory cardiac monitoring has no indication.

Back to baseline with a normal examination, no head injury (she slid from the chair) and no anticoagulation: emergency CT is not indicated, and the epilepsy-protocol MRI answers the structural question.
FDG-PET adds nothing to a first diagnosis with concordant MRI and EEG; it belongs to presurgical evaluation of drug-resistant epilepsy.

accepted: Focal epilepsy of left temporal lobe origin (dysembryoplastic neuroepithelial tumor)

differential.key_features: Imaging cannot reliably separate ganglioglioma from DNET; the absent enhancement, multicystic cortical pattern and inner table scalloping favor DNET; histology decides.

differential.diagnosis: Focal cortical dysplasia (type IIIb, associated with low-grade tumor)
differential.key_features: FCD may accompany a DNET at the lesion margin (type IIIb); this is a histological diagnosis made at resection.
The small size and benign appearance could prompt dismissal, but the cortical location and the concordant left temporal EEG focus make it the epileptogenic substrate.
Excluded: hippocampi normal in volume (left 3.1, right 3.2 cm3), signal and internal architecture; the lesion is neocortical.
Suggested by the patient; no diabetes or glucose-lowering drug, glucose 88 mg/dL, and the episodes are stereotyped with impaired awareness and automatisms.
Stereotyped gustatory and epigastric aura, witnessed automatisms, tongue bite, concordant EEG and a structural lesion are not PNES.

key_clinical_evidence: Six to eight stereotyped metallic taste and rising epigastric auras in ten months, two witnessed with impaired awareness and automatisms, are prior focal seizures, so the two-seizure criterion for epilepsy is met [ILAE_def_2014].
Left anterior temporal spike-and-wave discharges on EEG are concordant with the left inferior temporal cortical lesion with DNET features; its small size does not make it incidental.

Unilateral manual automatisms are usually ipsilateral to the onset, so the right-hand picking is a weak, discordant sign that does not outweigh the concordant left temporal EEG focus and left temporal lesion; the side of a tongue bite does not lateralize [Lateralization_2005].
Epilepsy-associated glioneuronal tumors have among the best seizure outcomes after resection, so surgical evaluation is appropriate at diagnosis [Blumcke_2017].
In a woman of childbearing potential without current contraception, a non-inducing first-line ASM (lamotrigine or levetiracetam) keeps future hormonal contraception reliable [NICE_NG217_2025].

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A cortically-based bubbly T2-hyperintense left temporal lesion without enhancement is the classical MRI appearance of DNET; small size and lack of mass effect are characteristic features, not evidence of non-epileptogenicity. Concordance with left anterior temporal EEG localizes this lesion as the epileptogenic substrate.
red_herrings.data_point: Left inferior temporal cortical lesion measuring only 14 x 11 x 10 mm (about 0.8 cm3) without mass effect, edema or enhancement
red_herrings.intended_effect: An agent may interpret the small size and entirely benign imaging appearance of the lesion as evidence that it is a non-epileptogenic incidental developmental anomaly, and proceed to search for an alternative explanation for the seizures.

general.query: focal epilepsy in adults: definition, classification, imaging and first-line treatment

results.finding: Epilepsy is present after at least two unprovoked seizures more than 24 hours apart, after one unprovoked seizure with a recurrence risk of at least 60% over the next 10 years, or when an epilepsy syndrome is diagnosed.
results.source: Fisher RS et al., Epilepsia 2014;55:475-482 | ILAE official report: a practical clinical definition of epilepsy

results.finding: Seizures are classified by onset as focal, generalized or unknown; focal seizures are described by awareness and by their first motor or non-motor feature, and may evolve to focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizures.
results.source: Fisher RS et al., Epilepsia 2017;58:522-530 | Operational classification of seizure types by the International League Against Epilepsy: position paper of the ILAE Commission for Classification and Terminology

results.finding: A harmonized epilepsy MRI protocol (3D T1 and 3D FLAIR at about 1 mm isotropic resolution and high-resolution coronal T2) is recommended for adults with focal epilepsy; non-dedicated protocols miss subtle lesions.
results.source: Bernasconi A et al., Epilepsia 2019;60:1054-1068 | Recommendations for the use of structural magnetic resonance imaging in the care of patients with epilepsy: a consensus report from the International League Against Epilepsy Neuroimaging Task Force

results.finding: Lamotrigine or levetiracetam is offered as first-line monotherapy for focal seizures, with carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, zonisamide or lacosamide as further options.
results.source: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence, NG217 2022 | Epilepsies in children, young people and adults

results.finding: Drug-resistant epilepsy is failure of adequate trials of two tolerated, appropriately chosen and used antiseizure medication schedules to achieve sustained seizure freedom.
results.source: Kwan P et al., Epilepsia 2010;51:1069-1077 | Definition of drug resistant epilepsy: consensus proposal by the ad hoc Task Force of the ILAE Commission on Therapeutic Strategies

general.summary: Epilepsy is diagnosed after two unprovoked seizures more than 24 hours apart or one with a high recurrence risk, and focal seizures are classified by onset and awareness (ILAE 2014, 2017). A dedicated epilepsy-protocol MRI is the imaging of choice (ILAE 2019). Lamotrigine or levetiracetam is first-line monotherapy for focal seizures (NICE NG217), and drug resistance is failure of two appropriate medication schedules (ILAE 2010).

patient.history_present_illness:
Ms. Kapoor is a 24-year-old right-handed South Asian female graduate student in biochemistry who was brought to the emergency department by her roommate after a witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure that occurred in their shared apartment this morning. Her roommate reports that the patient was sitting at her desk reading when she suddenly stopped and stared blankly ahead. She did not respond when her name was called. Her right hand began picking repetitively at the sleeve of her sweater, and she appeared to make chewing motions with her mouth. After approximately 25 seconds of this unresponsive behavior, she slid off the chair to the floor and developed bilateral limb stiffening followed by rhythmic jerking of all four extremities lasting approximately 60 to 70 seconds. The roommate called emergency services. Paramedics found the patient confused and unable to follow commands. On arrival to the emergency department approximately 40 minutes after the event, she was drowsy but arousable and increasingly coherent.

On interview, the patient reports that immediately before losing awareness she experienced an unusual metallic taste that she cannot otherwise characterize, accompanied by a rising warmth that started in her abdomen and moved upward into her chest. She felt briefly detached from her surroundings before the episode ended her memory. She has no recollection of anything until she found herself on the floor with paramedics present.

She reports that she has experienced similar episodes of the metallic taste with the rising abdominal sensation approximately six to eight times over the past ten months. These events have lasted 20 to 45 seconds and resolved spontaneously, leaving her mildly confused and fatigued. On two occasions, her roommate told her she appeared to be staring and unresponsive, and once seemed to be chewing and fidgeting with her hands, though the patient has no memory of these observations. She dismissed all episodes as stress or hypoglycemia related to long study hours and did not seek medical attention. She denies any prior history of unprovoked seizures, febrile convulsions, head trauma, encephalitis, or meningitis. She has had no recent illness, fever, or significant sleep deprivation beyond her usual graduate student schedule. Her last menstrual period was three weeks ago. She is not on any hormonal contraception. She takes loratadine occasionally but has not used it this week.

Facial movements symmetric at rest and with volitional activation. Hearing intact bilaterally to finger rub. Palate elevates symmetrically; uvula midline. Gag reflex present bilaterally. Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius strength 5/5 bilaterally. Tongue protrudes midline without atrophy or fasciculations.
